knowledge_points.label: The data-movement hierarchy extends across GPUs and nodes
knowledge_points.statement: Compute is far from data at every level, and each level is slower: L1/shared memory → HBM (8 TB/s on B200) → NVLink/NVSwitch within a node (1.8 TB/s) → Infiniband across nodes (~0.05 TB/s) → Ethernet across pods; last week's fusion/tiling and this week's replication/sharding are the same move at different levels.

anchors.quote: compute (arithmetic logic units) is far from inputs/outputs (data). Unifying theme: orchestrate computation to avoid data transfer bottlenecks
Generalized hierarchy: ... L1 cache / shared memory (fastest) ... HBM ... NVLink/NVSwitch ... Infiniband/Ethernet (slowest)
8 GPUs per node, connected by NVLink to an NVSwitch (B200s' NVLink 5.0 gets 1.8 TB/s; HBM was 8 TB/s) ... Infiniband ... (~0.05 TB/s)
PCI(e) bus (v7.0, 16 lanes => 242 GB/s) ... Ethernet (~200 MB/s)
GB200/GB300 NVL72: 8 GPUs per tray, 9 trays per rack -> 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain
taking a little bit of liberty, we can think about the generalized hierarchy ... HBM, which we lamented was so slow. ... But in this lecture, HBM is going to be considered fast.

typically, you have eight GPUs per node. ... if you use NVLink 5, then you're getting 1.8 terabytes per second of total bandwidth. ... remember, HBM for B200 was 8 terabytes per second. ... So it's about 4x slower.

as your number of GPUs grows, then you're going to have to put these nodes into pods, which are connected by InfiniBand. ... you see that the speeds are much, much lower. ... You can't have an NVSwitch handling 100,000 GPUs.

normally, if you're mortal, you think, well OK, I have eight GPUs that are interlinked really fast. ... if you have a lot of money, you can buy this really fancy hardware and you can get really fast interconnects up to 72 GPUs.

let's say you have eight GPUs per node. ... So then the ninth one would be on a different node. ... that's going to be one node which is not providing that much compute and also very expensive to communicate with.

provenance.filtering_note: Bandwidths are single round numbers without derivation: the HBM figure is for B200 (lecture 5/6 used H100's 3.35 TB/s), the '~200 MB/s' Ethernet number is the home-network case (L213), and the PCIe figure comes from Wikipedia (L212). The professor uses them only to order the levels, not to compute anything. Spoken evidence (2:25, 24:03-24:08): the levels are relative to the lecture ('in this lecture, HBM is going to be considered fast'), and the numbers are used once aloud for a ratio: NVLink 5 at 1.8 TB/s against B200 HBM at 8 TB/s is 'about 4x slower' (8 / 1.8 = 4.4). This corrects the sentence above that the professor uses the bandwidths 'only to order the levels, not to compute anything': that ratio is the one computation. He also says the figure's '8 is typical, but this 256 is kind of made up' (23:35), gives the reason for the hierarchy, 'You can't have an NVSwitch handling 100,000 GPUs' (26:11), and presents NVL72 as moving the fast domain from 8 to 72 GPUs for those with 'a lot of money' (28:22-28:46). Spoken evidence (35:00-35:23, Q&A): a ninth GPU on another node without NVLink is 'really bad': little extra compute and expensive to reach. The tray answer (31:41-31:53: 'two CPUs. And each CPU is connected to four GPUs. So each tray has eight GPUs') matches L229's 8 per tray x 9 trays; NVIDIA's published GB200 NVL72 layout is 18 compute trays of 4 GPUs (author note, not anchored; flagged for review).

external_prerequisites.note: The first two levels (shared memory, HBM) are lecture 5's hierarchy; this KP appends NVLink and Infiniband below them.

misconceptions.belief: NVLink is about as fast as HBM, so spreading a model over 8 GPUs in a node is nearly free.
misconceptions.why_wrong: With the lecture's numbers NVLink 5.0 (1.8 TB/s) is ~4.4× slower than HBM (8 TB/s), and Infiniband (0.05 TB/s) is another ~36× slower; every level down costs an order of magnitude or so.

predict.q: Using only the lecture's numbers (HBM 8 TB/s, NVLink 5.0 1.8 TB/s, Infiniband ~0.05 TB/s): by what factor is NVLink slower than HBM, and Infiniband slower than NVLink?
predict.why: 8/1.8 ≈ 4.4; 1.8/0.05 = 36. Each hop down the hierarchy costs roughly an order of magnitude (L219-L220).
predict.targets_misconception: NVLink is about as fast as HBM, so spreading a model over 8 GPUs in a node is nearly free.

transfer.q: A 16 GB gradient tensor must cross one link. With the lecture's bandwidths, how long does it take over NVLink 5.0 (1.8 TB/s) versus Infiniband (0.05 TB/s)? Give both in milliseconds.
transfer.why: 16/1800 s ≈ 0.0089 s; 16/50 s = 0.32 s. Same bytes, 36× the time: this is why the summary says tensor parallelism wants NVLink and pipeline parallelism can tolerate slow links (L69-L70).

check.q: Using the lecture's bandwidths (HBM 8 TB/s on B200, NVLink 5.0 1.8 TB/s), reading a tensor out of one GPU's HBM takes 0.9 ms. How many milliseconds does sending the same tensor to another GPU in the node over NVLink 5.0 take?
check.why: Transfer time is bytes / bandwidth, so the time scales by the inverse bandwidth ratio: 0.9 ms × 8 / 1.8 = 4.0 ms. One hop down the hierarchy (HBM to NVLink) already costs about 4.4× (L219).
check.varies: the pair of levels compared (HBM vs NVLink instead of NVLink vs Infiniband) and the given quantity (a time, not a byte count)
check.invariant: time = bytes / bandwidth, so the time ratio between two levels is the inverse of their bandwidth ratio
check.targets_misconception: NVLink is about as fast as HBM, so spreading a model over 8 GPUs in a node is nearly free.

retrieval.q: List the four levels of the lecture's generalized data-movement hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
retrieval.answer: L1 cache / shared memory; HBM; NVLink/NVSwitch (multi-GPU, one node); Infiniband/Ethernet (multi-node) (L29-L32).

retrieval.q: What one-sentence 'unifying theme' does the professor give for both single-GPU and multi-GPU work?
retrieval.answer: Orchestrate computation to avoid data-transfer bottlenecks, because compute is far from data (L25-L26).

retrieval.q: How many GPUs share one NVLink domain in a GB200 NVL72 rack? Type only the number.
retrieval.answer: 72. NVIDIA's published GB200 NVL72 layout is 18 compute trays × 4 GPUs; the lecture (L229, and aloud at 31:41) says 8 per tray × 9 trays, which gives the same total.

presentations.notice: For the same bytes, each hop down the ladder multiplies the time by a fixed factor, whatever the payload: about 4.4x from HBM to NVLink and 36x from NVLink to Infiniband.

Leaving the node costs a bigger factor than leaving the chip did.
The ratios multiply down the hierarchy, so the traffic that crosses nodes should be the smallest (the summary puts tensor parallelism on NVLink and lets pipeline parallelism use slow links).

knowledge_points.label: Ranks, world size, and the collective-operation vocabulary
knowledge_points.statement: A collective is one communication pattern specified over all ranks (rank = one device, world size = number of devices); broadcast/scatter/gather/reduce are the foundations, all-gather/reduce-scatter/all-reduce the workhorses, all-to-all the most general; 'reduce' applies an associative op, 'scatter' is the inverse of gather, and 'all-' means the destination is every rank.

anchors.quote: Collective means that you specify a general communication pattern across many devices. This can be better/faster than managing point-to-point communication yourself.
Rank: a particular device/GPU (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3). World size: total number of devices (e.g., 4)
Broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce (foundations). All-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce (workhorse). All-to-all (for MoEs)
Reduce: performs some associative/commutative operation (sum, min, max). Scatter is inverse of gather. All: means destination is all devices
rank0 = tensor([6.])  # Sum of all ranks (0 + 1 + 2 + 3)
collective operations are these primitives from distributed programming that go back to the '80s. ... It wasn't invented for LLM training.
So the first three, broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce, are really just warm ups, I would say. ... All gather, reduce scatter, and all reduce are the ones that are going to show up again and again
So you can think about gather as a reduction where the operation is concatenation, if you will.
You'll see later in the code, you basically specify the GPU ID or the rank and it goes there.
So the inverse of scatter is scatter. ... So this should be very predictable.

provenance.filtering_note: The four foundations are shown as literal 4-rank tensors (L91-L137) with no code run; the professor calls them stepping stones and spends the real time on the three workhorses. Broadcast's use case is reduced to 'rank 0 loads a checkpoint' (L101). Spoken evidence (5:56, 7:37): the collectives are introduced as old parallel-programming primitives ('go back to the '80s'), and the four foundations are 'really just warm ups'. Spoken evidence (11:26): gather is 'a reduction where the operation is concatenation', which ties the gather and reduce rows together. Q&A (20:48-21:10): the destination rank of a gather or reduce is an argument of the call, not fixed in advance; (12:06-12:27) broadcast matches NumPy broadcasting only as the idea of 'one thing that goes to many things'. Spoken slip (10:13): 'So the inverse of scatter is scatter'; the next sentences describe gather, and L205 and his own mnemonic at 20:07 say 'Scatter is the inverse gather'. Not imported.

misconceptions.belief: Gather and reduce are the same thing: both bring data to rank 0.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Gather concatenates the pieces (rank 0 ends with [0,1,2,3], length = world size); reduce combines them with an op (rank 0 ends with [6], same length as each input) (L115-L135).

predict.q: Four ranks each hold a length-1 tensor containing their rank. After a gather to rank 0, versus a reduce(SUM) to rank 0, what does rank 0 hold in each case?
predict.why: Gather concatenates (length grows to world size); reduce applies the op across ranks (length unchanged) (L117-L123, L129-L135).
predict.targets_misconception: Gather and reduce are the same thing: both bring data to rank 0.

transfer.q: World size 8; each rank holds the length-1 tensor [rank]. Give the shape and contents of rank 0 after reduce with op=MAX, and after gather.
transfer.why: Reduce keeps the input shape and applies the associative op (max of 0..7 = 7); gather's output length is world size × input length (L204-L205).

check.q: World size 6; each rank holds a length-3 tensor. After reduce with op=SUM to rank 0, how many elements does rank 0's result tensor have?
check.why: Reduce applies the associative op elementwise across ranks and keeps the input shape, so the result has 3 elements; a gather would instead concatenate 6 × 3 = 18 elements (L204-L205).
check.varies: world size (6), tensor length (3), op (SUM); asks only for the output length
check.invariant: reduce keeps the input shape; gather multiplies the length by the world size
check.targets_misconception: Gather and reduce are the same thing: both bring data to rank 0.

retrieval.q: Define 'rank' and 'world size' in one phrase each.
retrieval.answer: Rank: the index of one device/process; world size: the total number of devices (L83-L84).

retrieval.q: Name the three 'workhorse' collectives the professor contrasts with the four 'foundations'.
retrieval.answer: All-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce (L88).

retrieval.q: In the professor's mnemonic, what does the prefix 'all-' change about an operation?
retrieval.answer: The destination: the result lands on every rank instead of only rank 0 (L206).

prompts.self_explain: Why might a library collective beat hand-written point-to-point sends even though both move the same bytes?

presentations.notice: Gather's output on rank 0 is W times as long as one input; reduce's output keeps the input length, and each of its cells outlines one input cell from every rank.

knowledge_points.label: All-gather: every rank ends with the concatenation of all shards
knowledge_points.statement: All-gather is gather to every rank: W shards of length n become the same length-W·n tensor on every rank, with nothing summed; its training use is assembling full parameters from parameter shards before a forward pass.

anchors.quote: All-gather: perform gather to all ranks, not just rank 0 ... rank3 = tensor([0., 1, 2, 3])
Use case: each rank holds parameter shard, gather to get full parameters for forward pass
output = torch.empty(world_size, ...) ... dist.all_gather_into_tensor(output_tensor=output, input_tensor=input, async_op=False)
Rank 2 [after all-gather]: input = tensor([14.], device='cuda:2'), output = tensor([ 6., 10., 14., 18.], device='cuda:2')
all gather is what you do to-- basically, you perform gather to all ranks, not just rank 0. ... And now all gather just does it for every single rank.

later we'll see that each rank holds part of the parameters. ... all gather the parameters to get the full parameters for the full forward pass. ... we're going to see a lot of this gather to do something and then scatter and then gather and scatter again.
The output is just allocated. ... It happens to have some values in it, but don't worry about it.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture shows only equal-sized shards and the SUM-free semantics; the 'before all-gather' stdout lines show torch.empty garbage in the output buffer (L40-L43 of the trace), which the professor does not comment on. Spoken evidence (13:32): the pattern to expect in training is 'gather to do something and then scatter and then gather and scatter again'. Correction (45:28-45:37): the note above says the garbage in the 'before all-gather' output buffer gets no comment; it gets one line: 'The output is just allocated. It happens to have some values in it, but don't worry about it.' (Likewise for reduce-scatter at 42:49: the output 'happens to be zeros, but it could be just anything'.)

misconceptions.belief: All-gather sums the shards.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It concatenates; nothing is reduced. In the lecture's example 0, 1, 2, 3 become [0, 1, 2, 3] on every rank, not 6 (L141-L150).

predict.q: World size 4; rank r holds the length-2 tensor [r, r]. After all-gather, what tensor does rank 2 hold?
predict.why: Shards are concatenated in rank order on every rank; rank 2's output is the same as rank 0's (L139-L150).

transfer.q: World size 8; each rank holds a shard of 1,000,000 bf16 parameters. After all-gather, how many MB of parameters does each rank hold, and how many of those MB arrived from other ranks?
transfer.why: 8 × 1e6 × 2 bytes = 16 MB on every rank; 7/8 of it (14 MB) came over the interconnect, only the rank's own 2 MB shard was local. This is the per-layer cost ZeRO-3/FSDP pays to run a forward pass (L152).

check.q: World size 4; each rank holds a shard of 3,000,000 fp32 parameters (4 bytes each). After all-gather, how many MB on each rank arrived from the other ranks? Use 1 MB = 10^6 bytes and do not count the rank's own shard.
check.why: Every rank ends with 4 × 3e6 × 4 B = 48 MB; its own 12 MB shard was already local, so 3 × 12 = 36 MB came over the interconnect. Nothing is summed: a summing collective would leave only 12 MB per rank.
check.varies: world size 4, fp32 instead of bf16, and only the received bytes are asked
check.invariant: all-gather leaves W × shard on every rank, of which (W − 1)/W arrives from other ranks

retrieval.q: Which torch.distributed call does the lecture use for all-gather into a preallocated tensor, and how long must the output be relative to the input?
retrieval.answer: all_gather_into_tensor; world_size × the input length (L276, L279).

retrieval.q: State the sharded-training use case the professor attaches to all-gather.
retrieval.answer: Each rank holds a parameter shard; all-gather assembles the full parameters for the forward pass (L152).

prompts.self_explain: Why is the output of all-gather identical on every rank even though every rank's input differs?

presentations.notice: Every rank's output row is the same concatenation in rank order, and each output cell outlines exactly one input cell: nothing is summed.

knowledge_points.label: Reduce-scatter: sum each slot across ranks, deliver slot i to rank i
knowledge_points.statement: In reduce-scatter every rank holds a full-length vector; slot i is reduced across all ranks and only rank i receives that result (W inputs of length W·n → one length-n shard per rank), so gradients from data shards get summed while the storage is distributed.

anchors.quote: rank1 = tensor([10.]) # Sum along dim 1 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)
Use case: after backward pass, sum gradients from different data shards, but distribute storage
output = torch.empty(1, ...) ... dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(output=output, input=input, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
Rank 3 [after reduce-scatter]: input = tensor([3., 4., 5., 6.], device='cuda:3'), output = tensor([18.], device='cuda:3')

But now reduce scatter says that for each component of this tensor, I'm going to do a reduction, and then I'm going to put it on a different rank. ... So the first dimension, I'm going to add these up, I get 6.

after the backward pass, when you sum what you're going to do is each GPU will be dealing with different data. ... you need to sum all of the gradients from the different shards. ... And then you're going to redistribute this storage.
Here instead of writing in place, I have an output tensor and an input tensor. ... the input is not touched, but the output I get the reduction of each component written into the respective ranks.

provenance.filtering_note: Scatter (L103-L113) is introduced only as a stepping stone to this. The professor shows SUM only; MIN/MAX are mentioned in the mnemonic (L204) but never run. Spoken evidence (43:08-43:13): unlike all_reduce, which 'writes in place to the data' (41:21), reduce_scatter_tensor takes a separate output and leaves its input untouched, and the output buffer's initial contents do not matter (42:49).

misconceptions.belief: After reduce-scatter every rank holds the full summed vector.
misconceptions.why_wrong: That is all-reduce. After reduce-scatter rank i holds only slot i's sum: rank 1 holds [10], not [6, 10, 14, 18] (L162-L165).

predict.q: The lecture's inputs: rank r holds [r, r+1, r+2, r+3] for r = 0..3. After reduce-scatter(SUM), what single number does rank 3 hold?
predict.why: Slot 3 across the four ranks is 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18, delivered only to rank 3 (L165).
predict.targets_misconception: After reduce-scatter every rank holds the full summed vector.

transfer.q: World size 3; rank 0 holds [1, 2, 3], rank 1 holds [10, 20, 30], rank 2 holds [100, 200, 300]. After reduce-scatter(SUM), what does rank 1 hold?
transfer.why: Rank 1 receives the reduction of slot 1: 2 + 20 + 200 = 222; rank 0 would get 111 and rank 2 would get 333. Output length is input length / world size = 1.

retrieval.q: After reduce-scatter over world size W on inputs of length L, what is the length of each rank's output?
retrieval.answer: L / W (L265-L266: input arange(world_size), output empty(1)).

retrieval.q: The professor gives the same gradient use case for reduce-scatter and all-reduce; which word differs?
retrieval.answer: Reduce-scatter: sum gradients but *distribute* storage; all-reduce: sum gradients but *replicate* full parameters (L167 vs L182).

prompts.self_explain: Why is reduce-scatter the natural primitive when gradients must be summed but no single rank needs the whole gradient?

presentations.notice: Rank i's one output cell outlines slot i on every input rank: one value from each rank, summed, delivered only to rank i.

knowledge_points.label: All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather
knowledge_points.statement: All-reduce leaves every rank with the full elementwise reduction and is exactly reduce-scatter followed by all-gather; the lecture feeds the reduce-scatter output into an all-gather and reproduces the all-reduce result, and that split is what lets ZeRO/FSDP keep state sharded between the two halves.

anchors.quote: All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather ... Breaking all-reduce into reduce-scatter + all-gather allows for flexibility (e.g., ZeRO/FSDP)
input = output  # Input is the output of reduce-scatter ... Indeed, all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather!
all-reduce moves 2x the data in 2x the time compared to reduce-scatter, so similar bandwidth
Rank 0 [after all-reduce]: tensor([ 6., 10., 14., 18.])
it's basically you do one and then you do the other. ... And the all gather part of all reduce just puts them all on the same-- everything on the same node.

Later, we're going to see how to get to fancier things like 0 or FSDP. ... We need to break the all reduce into reduce scatter and all gather, because then you can intervene and you can manage things a bit more.
it would be gloo, but it could be NCCL, in which case, it would spin up the Cuda kernels. ... And then it basically writes in place to the data.
proof via example that all reduce is equal to reduce scatter plus all gather.

all reduce, naturally, is moving twice the amount of data, because reduce scatter has some cost, all gather has some cost ... And it takes twice the amount of time. ... But the two cancel out, so you get the same kind of bandwidth.

provenance.filtering_note: The identity is demonstrated on a 4-element example and asserted for cost (L369-L370); the professor does not show the ring algorithm that makes each half cost S·(W−1)/W per rank. The nccl-tests PERFORMANCE.md link (L297) carries that derivation. Spoken evidence (16:32-16:41): the reason to split all-reduce is control, 'because then you can intervene and you can manage things a bit more', said before the code's ZeRO/FSDP line. Spoken evidence (52:40-53:06): L369-L370 aloud: twice the data and twice the time, so 'the two cancel out, so you get the same kind of bandwidth'. The ring algorithm is still not described; 'a ring or a tree topology' is named once as NCCL's choice (51:19).

misconceptions.belief: All-reduce is a single cheap primitive; reduce-scatter and all-gather are separate, extra operations.
misconceptions.why_wrong: NCCL's all-reduce is implemented as the two halves; each half moves half the bytes, so running both halves yourself costs the same as the all-reduce (L369-L370).

predict.q: Rank r holds [r, r+1, r+2, r+3] for r = 0..3. After reduce-scatter(SUM) each rank holds one number; an all-gather then runs on those. What does rank 0 hold at the end, and how does it compare with all-reduce(SUM) on the original inputs?
predict.why: Reduce-scatter yields 6, 10, 14, 18 on ranks 0..3; all-gather concatenates them on every rank, which is exactly what all-reduce produces (L171-L180, L275-L282).
predict.targets_misconception: All-reduce is a single cheap primitive; reduce-scatter and all-gather are separate, extra operations.

transfer.q: World size 2; rank 0 holds [1, 2] and rank 1 holds [3, 4]. Write what each rank holds after reduce-scatter(SUM), and then after the following all-gather.
transfer.answer: after reduce-scatter: rank 0 [4], rank 1 [6]; after all-gather: both [4, 6]
transfer.why: Slot 0: 1 + 3 = 4 goes to rank 0; slot 1: 2 + 4 = 6 goes to rank 1; all-gather concatenates in rank order, giving the all-reduce answer [4, 6] everywhere.

check.q: World size 3. Rank 0 holds [1, 0, 4], rank 1 holds [0, 3, 1], rank 2 holds [2, 1, 0]. They run reduce-scatter(SUM) and then an all-gather on its output. What is the last element (index 2) of rank 0's final tensor?
check.why: Reduce-scatter gives slot 2's sum 4 + 1 + 0 = 5 to rank 2 (rank 0 keeps only slot 0's sum, 3). The all-gather then copies every slot to every rank, so rank 0 ends with [3, 4, 5], the same as all-reduce(SUM).
check.varies: world size 3, and the element asked for is one rank 0 did not own after the reduce-scatter
check.invariant: all-reduce = reduce-scatter (each rank owns one fully reduced slot) followed by all-gather (every rank gets every slot)

retrieval.q: Complete, in order: all-reduce = ____ followed by ____.
retrieval.answer: reduce-scatter, then all-gather (L169, L282).

retrieval.q: Which systems does the professor name as the reason to care that all-reduce decomposes?
retrieval.answer: ZeRO/FSDP: between the two halves, parameters and gradients can stay sharded (L183, L68).

prompts.self_explain: If all-reduce is reduce-scatter then all-gather, where in a data-parallel step could you stop halfway and still have a correct algorithm, and what would you have saved?

presentations.notice: After the first W-1 ring steps each rank owns one fully summed slot (the reduce-scatter result 6, 10, 14, 18); the next W-1 steps only copy those slots, ending with the all-reduce on every rank.
With 'reduce-scatter, then all-gather' the middle grid holds one sum per rank, and the final grid is identical to all-reduce on the same inputs.

knowledge_points.label: All-to-all: each rank sends chunk j to rank j (a transpose)
knowledge_points.statement: In all-to-all, rank i sends its j-th chunk to rank j and receives the i-th chunk of every rank, so with balanced chunks the W×W rank-by-chunk layout is transposed; it is the routing primitive for MoE, where data is split across ranks and experts are split across ranks.

anchors.quote: rank1 = tensor([4., 5, 6, 7])      # send  4 to rank 0,  5 to rank 1,  6 to rank 2,  7 to rank 3 ... rank1 = tensor([1, 5, 9, 13])
Useful for MoEs: each rank has split of data and subset of experts; need to route data to experts. For balanced splits, all-to-all looks like transpose
So basically, the position here is going to denote which rank is going to be the ultimate destination. ... the first rank is going to receive everyone who sent everything in column 0

each rank has both a split of the data and also a subset of experts. ... the key idea of the MOE is that it's dynamic routing. ... You have to look at your data to figure out which experts you need to route those activations to.
But in general, all to all also handles unbalanced splits. ... But in general, you want the splits to be as balanced as possible. ... MOE lecture where we had load balancing

provenance.filtering_note: Shown only as a static example; never run in torch.distributed and no bytes are counted. The unbalanced-split case is mentioned in one line (L201). Spoken evidence (18:29-18:44): why MoE needs all-to-all rather than a fixed pattern: 'the key idea of the MOE is that it's dynamic routing', so which rank receives which activations is known only after looking at the data. Spoken evidence (19:08-19:34): unbalanced splits are supported but not shown, and the goal is balance, tied back to the MoE lecture's load balancing (lecture_04 thread). knowledge_points.label: RDMA bypasses the CPU; NCCL turns collectives into GPU kernels
knowledge_points.statement: Standard Ethernet routes GPU-to-GPU traffic through the CPU (kernel socket buffer, TCP packets, NIC ring buffer); RDMA lets one GPU read or write another GPU's memory without the CPU — Infiniband supports it, plain Ethernet does not, RoCE adds it to Ethernet more cheaply — and NCCL implements collectives by detecting the topology, optimizing the path between GPUs, and launching GPU kernels that send and receive.

RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE): Ethernet bypasses CPU, similar but cheaper/weaker than Infiniband, used by Meta
NCCL translates collective operations into low-level packets ... Detects topology ... Optimizes the path between GPUs ... Launches GPU kernels to send/receive data
Supports multiple backends for different hardware: gloo (CPU), nccl (GPU)

if you have traditional ethernet, what happens is that the GPU has to talk to the CPU to get its data copied. ... Here kernel means not the GPU kernel, but the CPU, traditional notion of a kernel. ... So this generally introduces a lot of latency.

Remote Direct Memory Access, RDMA, which allows a GPU to directly write or read from another GPU's memory without using the CPU at all. ... InfiniBand also supports RDMA. ... But standard ethernet does not.
So InfiniBand generally is very expensive, as is a lot of NVIDIA products. ... But you can get pretty good performance by using RDMA over converged ethernet.

NCCL goes and figures out what is the topology of the hardware, figures out the path between different GPUs, and then it actually launches the GPU kernels to send and receive data. ... everything that runs on a GPU is a kernel.

So RDMA, you can think about it as more of a desiderata. ... So InfiniBand and NVSwitch and NVLink are more the hardware, what pieces, what cables and switches are there. ... And RDMA is more operation, what happens when you're communicating.

knowledge_points.label: Byte accounting for all-reduce and reduce-scatter
knowledge_points.statement: The lecture's effective bandwidth for an all-reduce of S bytes per rank counts sent_bytes = 2·S·(W−1) (send + receive over W−1 steps) over W·duration rank-seconds, so bandwidth ≈ 2·S/duration, independent of world size and of ring vs tree; a reduce-scatter of S_in bytes per rank sends S_in·(W−1) with no factor 2, so for the same input it moves half the bytes of an all-reduce.

anchors.quote: sent_bytes = size_bytes * 2 * (world_size - 1)  # 2x because send + receive, world_size-1 steps in all-reduce ... total_duration = world_size * duration

spawn(all_reduce, world_size=4, num_elements=100 * 1024**2) ... spawn(reduce_scatter, world_size=4, num_elements=100 * 1024**2)

analogous to when we were computing MFU, is to measure the effective bandwidth. ... compute essentially how many bytes were sent and should be sent during this computation.
You need to iterate this world size minus 1 steps, because there's a world size minus 1 addition operations. ... There's a 2, because you need to both send and reduce.
And then you multiply by the world size, because it's the total amount that all the ranks have waited.

as world size increases, this world size minus 1 divided by world size essentially converges to 1. ... Notice that this is independent of the world size, which is good. ... It is also independent of the topology

knowledge_points.label: Naive data parallelism: shard the batch, all-reduce the gradients
knowledge_points.statement: In naive data parallelism (DDP) every rank keeps a full copy of parameters and optimizer state, processes batch/W of the data and computes its own loss, then all-reduces (AVG) every gradient so that after optimizer.step() the parameters stay identical on all ranks; the only communication per step is one all-reduce of the full gradient.

anchors.quote: Sharding strategy: each rank gets a slice of the data
local_batch_size = int_divide(batch_size, world_size) ... data = data[start_index:end_index]
each rank has all parameters ... Each rank has own optimizer state
Sync gradients across workers (ONLY difference between standard training and DDP) ... dist.all_reduce(tensor=param.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.AVG, async_op=False)
Losses are different across ranks (computed on local data). Gradients are all-reduced to be the same across ranks. Therefore, parameters remain the same across ranks. Next time: FSDP/ZeRO
Now, in practice, each rank should probably load its own data rather than have this bottleneck, but this is just for illustrative purposes.
it's basically standard training where you apply it to your local batch, but you just insert this after the backward pass. ... It's a one line code change, and then the parameters get updated.
So your batch size has to be at least world size for this to really make sense. ... I mean, if it's not, then you can pad it with zeros or something.
It would actually be basically the same. ... The DDP has the nice thing that is very modular. ... I mean, DDP just averages the parameters here. ... It doesn't care what your forward pass looks like.
here we use all reduce. ... It's a very simple monolithic operation, but it does require holding all the models, parameters in memory.
But if you're clever, then on the backward pass, as soon as the gradients are done, you can start sending that. ... And that's something that will be explored in the assignment two.

You're doing redundant work in some sense, because every rank is actually updating its parameters and keeping track of all the parameters. ... But the reason you're doing that is that you don't have to move the optimizer state across.

knowledge_points.label: ZeRO/FSDP: shard optimizer state, gradients, then parameters
knowledge_points.statement: ZeRO/FSDP keeps the all-reduce split in two and shards state across the N data-parallel devices: with Ψ parameters in mixed precision (2 bytes fp16 param + 2 grad + K = 12 bytes of fp32 master copy and two Adam moments), replication costs 16Ψ per device; sharding optimizer state (stage 1) gives 4Ψ + 12Ψ/N, plus gradients (stage 2) 2Ψ + 14Ψ/N, plus parameters (stage 3) 16Ψ/N — paid for with an all-gather of parameters before use and a reduce-scatter of gradients after backward.

each rank holds parameter shard, gather to get full parameters for forward pass

knowledge_points.label: Tensor parallelism: shard the width, all-gather activations every layer
knowledge_points.statement: Tensor parallelism shards every layer's weight along its width: rank r holds the num_dim × (num_dim/W) column block of each layer, every rank holds the whole batch, computes a batch × (num_dim/W) activation slice, and the slices are all-gathered and concatenated after every layer — so communication is one full activation (batch × num_dim) per layer, which is why the summary says TP needs NVLink-class interconnect.

anchors.quote: Sharding strategy: each rank gets part of each layer, transfer all data/activations
All ranks get the data (batch_size x num_dim) ... local_num_dim = int_divide(num_dim, world_size) ... each rank gets 1/world_size of the parameters
x = x @ params[layer]  # Note: this is only on a slice of the parameters ... dist.all_gather(tensor_list=activations, tensor=x, async_op=False) ... x = torch.cat(activations, dim=1)
Tensor parallelism: requires very fast interconnects (e.g., NVLink)
[tensor_parallelism] Rank 0: forward pass produced activations 128x1024[4.0669...] ... [tensor_parallelism] Rank 3: forward pass produced activations 128x1024[4.0669...]
we're not going to cut the data. ... We're going to cut essentially each layer. ... And generally, this means that we're going to have to transfer a lot more data.
I would be splitting down the columns. ... So this is also known as column tensor parallel. ... You can also do it by rows, but we're not going to talk about that right now.

Data parallel is very elegant, because it's splitting by data. ... The model is treated as a module. ... But now we have to muck around with the model. ... if you want to do a matrix multiplication, you can split it up into a set of smaller matrix multiplications.

There's a lot of communication, because for every layer, you need to send all these activations, which are fairly big. ... So generally, tensor parallelism happens within a node on NVLink or where you have high bandwidth.

knowledge_points.label: Tensor parallel backward: forward all-gather pairs with reduce-scatter
knowledge_points.statement: In the lecture's column tensor parallelism each layer's forward pass ends with an all-gather of the activation slices, and the backward pass needs the dual collective, a reduce-scatter: every rank holds only a partial gradient for the full gathered activation (from its own column block of the next layer), so the partials must be summed and each rank keeps just the slice that its own weight block produced; forward all-gather pairs with backward reduce-scatter, and the reverse.

anchors.quote: Now, in the backprop, you have your activations and you have to reduce scatter to all the different gradients. ... all gather and reduce scatter have this kind of duality, where in forward, you're all gathering, in the backward, you're reduce scattering.
Here we're managing things fairly explicitly, which means I'm not doing the backward pass, but you would have to manage and call the reduce scatter yourself.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (1:08:08-1:08:33, in answer to a question; repeated at 1:09:14). The code stops at the forward pass ('# Backward pass: homework exercise', L479), so which collective the backward pass needs is not written anywhere in lecture_07.py; aloud: 'in forward, you're all gathering, in the backward, you're reduce scattering', and 'you would have to manage and call the reduce scatter yourself'. Why it is a reduce-scatter (each rank's downstream slice contributes a partial gradient to the whole gathered activation, the partials are summed, and each rank needs only its own slice) is the author's derivation, consistent with the collective definitions at L154-L167 and L139-L152. The reverse pairing used in the transfer (forward reduce-scatter, backward all-gather) is the same duality applied the other way; lecture 8 uses both directions in sequence parallelism (lecture_08:sequence-parallel). Placed after tensor-parallelism, where it is said. This states the answer to part of the homework, which the professor gives aloud; the implementation (shapes, autograd hooks) is still the homework.

Those partials must be summed (reduce), and each rank needs only the slice its weight block produced (scatter): a reduce-scatter (1:08:12-1:08:33).

Which collective does this layer's backward pass need for the gradient with respect to its input partials, and why?
transfer.answer: An all-gather: rank r receives the gradient for slice r only, but its partial output contributed to every slice, so each rank needs the full output gradient, which is gathered from all ranks.
transfer.why: The duality runs both ways: the backward of a sum-then-split (reduce-scatter) is a gather-to-everyone (all-gather), just as the backward of an all-gather is a reduce-scatter. Lecture 8's sequence parallelism uses exactly this pair.

knowledge_points.label: Pipeline parallelism: shard the depth, pass micro-batch activations point-to-point
knowledge_points.statement: Pipeline parallelism shards depth: rank r holds num_layers/W consecutive layers, the batch is cut into micro-batches, and each micro-batch's activations are passed with point-to-point dist.recv from rank r−1 and dist.send to rank r+1; only stage boundaries communicate, so slow links are tolerable, but stages idle while waiting (the bubble).

anchors.quote: Sharding strategy: each rank gets subset of layers, transfer all data/activations
local_num_layers = int_divide(num_layers, world_size) ... Each rank gets a subset of layers
Break up into micro batches to minimize the bubble ... micro_batch_size = int_divide(batch_size, num_micro_batches)
dist.recv(tensor=x, src=rank - 1) ... for param in local_params: x = x @ param ... dist.send(tensor=x, dst=rank + 1)
Pipeline parallelism: can work with slow interconnects, but need to work to reduce pipeline bubbles
[pipeline_parallelism] Rank 0: sending 32x1024[0.2459...] to rank 1 ... [pipeline_parallelism] Rank 0: sending 32x1024[-0.1654...] to rank 1
the idea behind pipeline parallelism is we're going to split the network this way. ... So each rank is going to get a subset of the layers now.
So here I'm actually using these receive and send, which are pointwise operations. ... I'm going to receive this tensor from rank minus 1. ... And this says I'm going to send tensor x to rank plus 1.

overlapping communication and computation, which is actually very important to pipeline parallelism. ... If you put an I before these, then it becomes kind of async. ... So computation and communication should overlap.

Whereas a pipeline parallelism, you'll see people using it. ... this can tolerate much slower interconnects. ... some of the decentralized training work uses pipeline parallel, because your nodes are-- GPUs are halfway across the world.

knowledge_points.label: Four axes of parallelism and how they compose
knowledge_points.statement: Each strategy shards one axis of training — data parallelism the batch, tensor/expert parallelism the width, pipeline parallelism the depth, sequence parallelism the length — and they compose multiplicatively (W = W_d · W_t · W_p, each GPU holding 1/(W_t · W_p) of the parameters and 1/W_d of the batch); the summary's rules: DP = all-reduce (or ZeRO's all-gather + reduce-scatter), TP needs NVLink-class links, PP tolerates slow links but must fight bubbles, and any intermediate can be recomputed, stored, or stored on another GPU and communicated.

anchors.quote: Why do multi-GPU? 1. Your parameters (optimizer state + gradients + activations) don't fit on a single GPU. 2. You want to use more GPUs (more FLOPs) to train faster.

Many ways to parallelize: data (batch), tensor/expert (width), pipeline (depth), sequence (length) ... Can re-compute or store in memory or store in another GPUs memory and communicate

there's really two reasons. ... One is that your parameters or activations or gradients and optimizer state don't fit on the HBM memory of a single GPU. ... If you're training a 1 trillion parameter model, that's not going to fit on a single GPU.
which parallelism technique you choose is going to be strongly dependent on the hardware.

it will be tensor parallel within a node and then pipe data parallel or FSDP and then pipeline parallelism if you need it. ... But then you start hitting to something called the critical batch size, where if you start increasing the batch size too much, it doesn't actually help you

misconceptions.belief: The strategies compete for the same GPUs, so you pick one.
misconceptions.why_wrong: They cut different axes and compose: with W_t = 8 inside a node (NVLink), W_p = 4 across nodes, W_d = 32 replicas you use 1024 GPUs, each holding 1/32 of the parameters (L62, L67; Megatron 2021).

predict.q: A 1024-GPU job uses W_t = 8 (within each node), W_p = 4 and W_d = 32. Which axis does the fastest link (NVLink) carry, and what fraction of the parameters does one GPU hold (before any ZeRO)?
predict.answer: tensor parallelism on NVLink; 1/32 of the parameters
predict.why: TP moves a full activation every layer so it takes the 8-GPU NVLink domain (L69, L219); params are split by W_t · W_p = 32 and replicated W_d = 32 times.
predict.targets_misconception: The strategies compete for the same GPUs, so you pick one.

transfer.q: Same 1024 GPUs, now W_t = 8, W_p = 8, W_d = 16, with 160B parameters in bf16. How many GB of bf16 weights does one GPU hold?
transfer.why: 160e9 / (8 × 8) = 2.5e9 parameters per GPU × 2 B = 5 GB; each parameter is replicated W_d = 16 times. ZeRO would divide the replicated state by 16 on top of this.
